passages.happening:
The LORD speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai. “When you enter the land that I am giving you, the land itself must observe a Sabbath to the LORD” (verse 2).

“For six years you may sow your field and prune your vineyard and gather its crops” (verse 3). In the seventh year the fields are not sown and the vines are not pruned (verse 4). “The land must have a year of complete rest” (verse 5).

What grows by itself that year is food for everyone: the owner, his servants, the hired worker, the foreigner, the cattle and even the wild animals (verses 6-7).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 23 gave Israel a Sabbath every seventh day. This chapter gives the land a Sabbath every seventh year. The pattern of six and one, which began at creation, is now laid over the fields.

For a people who lived by farming, this was a large act of trust. A whole year without sowing meant living on what the land gave unasked, and on what had been stored. The law says so itself a few verses on, and answers the question with a promise (verses 20-22).

In that year the usual lines fell away. What grew was not harvested and sold by the owner. It was there for anyone to eat: the master and the servant, the citizen and the foreigner, the farm animal and the wild one. For one year in seven, the land fed everyone alike.

The reason comes later in the chapter: the land is God's. Israel farms it as his guest. A guest does not work his host's land to exhaustion.
passages.later:
Exodus gives the same law with the poor in view: in the seventh year the land is to rest, “so that the poor among your people may eat from the field” (Exodus 23:11).

The writer of Chronicles looks back on the exile and says that the land at last had the rest it had been refused: “So the land enjoyed its Sabbath rest all the days of the desolation” (2 Chronicles 36:21).
passages.asks: Israel was asked to stop working the land for a year and trust God for bread. Ask what you are afraid to stop doing, in case there is not enough. And ask how you treat the land and the things you own: as yours to use up, or as held in trust.

passages.happening:
Israel is to count seven times seven years. Then, on the Day of Atonement, a ram's horn is blown through the land (verses 8-9).

“So you are to consecrate the fiftieth year and proclaim liberty in the land for all its inhabitants. It shall be your Jubilee, when each of you is to return to his property and to his clan” (verse 10).

Because land comes back in the Jubilee, its price depends on how many harvests remain. “Do not take advantage of each other, but fear your God” (verse 17).

To the worry about food God answers, “I will send My blessing upon you in the sixth year, so that the land will yield a crop sufficient for three years” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
The Jubilee is among the boldest laws in the Bible. Every fiftieth year, land that a family had been forced to sell went back to that family, and Israelites who had sold themselves into service went home.

The name comes from the Hebrew yovel, a ram's horn, and so the year announced by its blast. The word for ‘liberty’, deror, is related to a word kings in Mesopotamia used when they cancelled debts and freed people held for debt, often at the start of a reign. Israel's law differs at one point. Release was not left to a king's good pleasure. It was fixed in the calendar and commanded by God.

It began on the Day of Atonement. On the day the people were made clean before God, the horn sounded and release was proclaimed in the land. Being put right with God and being set free belonged together.

The effect on buying and selling was simple. No one could really buy land. He bought the harvests until the next Jubilee. So no family could be shut out of the land for ever, and no one could go on adding field to field without limit.

Was the Jubilee ever kept? It is uncertain. The Old Testament has no clear record of one being proclaimed. Some scholars think it was an ideal that was never fully practiced; others think it was kept at times and not written down. Either way it shaped Israel's hope. In modern times the words of verse 10 were cast on the Liberty Bell in Philadelphia.
passages.later:
Isaiah uses the Jubilee's word for the work of God's anointed one: “to proclaim liberty to the captives and freedom to the prisoners, to proclaim the year of the LORD’s favor” (Isaiah 61:1-2).

Jesus read that passage in the synagogue at Nazareth and said, “Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:21).

Jeremiah tells of a release that was proclaimed in Jerusalem and then taken back. God's answer was severe: “You have not obeyed Me; you have not proclaimed freedom, each man for his brother and for his neighbor” (Jeremiah 34:17).
passages.asks: Every fifty years the losses of a lifetime were to be undone, and a family could begin again. Ask who around you is caught in a loss they cannot climb out of alone. And ask what debt, of money or of grievance, is in your power to release.

passages.happening:
“The land must not be sold permanently, because it is Mine, and you are but foreigners and residents with Me” (verse 23).

“If your brother becomes impoverished and sells some of his property, his nearest of kin may come and redeem what his brother has sold” (verse 25). If he has no one, but later prospers, he may buy it back himself (verses 26-27). If he cannot, it stays with the buyer until the Jubilee, and then returns (verse 28).

A house inside a walled city can be bought back only within a year. Village houses and the houses of the Levites return in the Jubilee (verses 29-34).
passages.hearers:
Verse 23 is the ground of the whole chapter. The land belongs to God. Israel lives on it as ‘foreigners and residents’ with him: as tenants and guests.

This turns round the usual way of thinking. The people who were told to love the foreigner are themselves foreigners on God's land. No Israelite could say of his field that it was his to do with as he pleased.

In a farming society, land was life. A family that lost its land lost its living, and often its freedom next. The chapter sets up three defenses against that slide. A close relative could buy the land back. The Hebrew verb is ga'al, to redeem, and the relative was called the go'el, the redeemer. Or the man himself could buy it back if his fortunes turned. And if neither happened, the Jubilee returned it anyway.

The law tells different kinds of property apart. A house in a walled town was more like goods for trade than a family farm, so it could be sold for good. A village house belonged with its fields. The Levites, who had no tribal land, always kept the right to buy back their houses.
passages.later:
The book of Ruth shows the law at work. Boaz, a relative, buys back the land of a dead man's family and marries his widow: “I am buying from Naomi all that belonged to Elimelech” (Ruth 4:9).

The prophets take the word for the relative who redeems and use it of God. Isaiah calls him Israel's Redeemer, the one who pays to set his family free.

Paul writes that God sent his Son, ‘born under the law, to redeem those under the law’ (Galatians 4:4-5). The link with the redeeming relative is one of theme. It is not a direct prediction.
passages.asks: God says the land is his. Ask what you hold, a house, savings, a business, that you speak of as simply yours. And ask who in your wider family or church has fallen on hard times, and whether you are the near relative who could help them back.

passages.happening:
“Now if your countryman becomes destitute and cannot support himself among you, then you are to help him as you would a foreigner or stranger, so that he can continue to live among you” (verse 35).

“Do not take any interest or profit from him, but fear your God” (verse 36). “You must not lend him your silver at interest or sell him your food for profit” (verse 37).

“I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt to give you the land of Canaan and to be your God” (verse 38).
passages.hearers:
The chapter is following a poor man down, step by step. First he sold some land. Now he has nothing left and cannot support himself.

The law's first word is ‘help him’. The aim is stated twice: that he may go on living ‘among you’. The poor man is not to be pushed out to the edge of the community or left to sink.

Then a ban. No interest on a loan to him, and no profit on food sold to him. A loan to such a man was a loan to someone in need. To charge interest on it was to make money from a neighbor's hunger. The law forbids it.

The reason is the exodus. God brought Israel out of Egypt and gave it a land. A people who received everything as a gift is not to trade on a brother's ruin.

This is not legal or financial advice for a modern reader. But the principle is not hard to see: no one should profit from another person's desperation.
passages.later:
Deuteronomy sets the goal high: “There will be no poor among you” (Deuteronomy 15:4).

After the exile, poor families cried out that they had been forced to pledge fields and even children for debt: “we are powerless to redeem them because our fields and vineyards belong to others” (Nehemiah 5:5). Nehemiah made the lenders give it back.

Luke says of the first church in Jerusalem, in words that echo Deuteronomy, “There were no needy ones among them” (Acts 4:34).
passages.asks: The law's first words about a ruined neighbor are ‘help him’, so that he can go on living among you. Ask who near you is one bad month from losing their footing. And ask whether any of your income comes from another person's desperation.

passages.happening:
“If a countryman among you becomes destitute and sells himself to you, then you must not force him into slave labor. Let him stay with you as a hired worker or temporary resident; he is to work for you until the Year of Jubilee” (verses 39-40). Then he and his children go free (verse 41).

“Because the Israelites are My servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt, they are not to be sold as slaves. You are not to rule over them harshly, but you shall fear your God” (verses 42-43).

Then the text says, “Your menservants and maidservants shall come from the nations around you, from whom you may purchase them” (verse 44). They may also be bought from foreigners living in the land. “These may become your property. You may leave them to your sons after you to inherit as property; you can make them slaves for life” (verses 45-46).
passages.hearers:
The poor man has reached the bottom. He has nothing left to sell but himself.

Even then the law holds him up. He is not to be treated as a slave. He is to be treated as a hired worker. His master may not ‘rule over them harshly’. And his service has an end. At the Jubilee he and his children go home to their own land.

The reason is one of the great sentences of the book. The Israelites are God's servants. He brought them out of Egypt. They already have a master, and so they cannot be owned by anyone else.

Then come verses 44 to 46, and an honest reader must stop. What the law forbids for an Israelite, it allows for a foreigner. A person from another nation could be bought, held for life, and left to one's children as property. The chapter draws a line, and the foreigner is on the wrong side of it.

The hard question below faces this.
passages.later:
Exodus limits the service of a Hebrew servant to six years (Exodus 21:2). This chapter goes further for a fellow Israelite who sells himself: he is to be treated as a hired worker.

Job saw that master and servant were made by one God: “Did not He who made me in the womb also make them? Did not the same One form us in the womb?” (Job 31:15).

Paul sent a runaway slave named Onesimus back to his master with a letter asking that he be received “no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother” (Philemon 1:16).
passages.hard:
Why does this chapter forbid making slaves of Israelites, and allow slaves from other nations to be held for life?

That question should be faced honestly, and these notes do not defend slavery.

Here is what the law permits. Verses 44 to 46 allow Israelites to buy slaves from the nations round about and from foreigners living among them, to hold them for life, and to leave them to their children as property. That is in the text, and it cannot be explained away.

Here is what the law limits. Kidnapping a person is a crime punished by death (Exodus 21:16). A master who maims a servant loses him (Exodus 21:26-27). An escaped slave is not to be sent back (Deuteronomy 23:15-16). The Sabbath rest was for servants too (Exodus 20:10). And this same book commands Israel to love the foreigner as itself (19:34). Many readers, among them Christopher Wright, read these laws the way Jesus read the divorce law: Moses permitted it ‘because of your hardness of heart’ (Matthew 19:8). A law can limit a harm in a fallen society without calling the harm good. Critics answer that the laws still allowed one person to own another, and that this has to be faced. Both things are true to the text.

Others point out that the chapter's own reasoning reaches further than the line it draws. If people belong to God and not to one another, that is true of every person he has made. The New Testament says that in Christ there is ‘neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free’ (Galatians 3:28), and it names ‘slave traders’ among those the law condemns (1 Timothy 1:10).

The history of these verses is painful. In the Atlantic slave trade and in the American South, slaveholders and many preachers used texts like these to defend slavery as biblical. That was a misuse, and it was wrong. Atlantic slavery was built on race and on kidnapping, and the law of Moses punished kidnapping with death. Christians who opposed slavery drew on the same Bible, on human dignity, the exodus and the gospel. The church's record was mixed, and it must be named honestly.

None of this makes verses 44 to 46 easy, and it should not. No one may use them to excuse the owning, the buying or the forced labor of any person.

A word for anyone who is being held, owned or forced to work today. It is not your fault. You are not the property of the people who hold you. If you can, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

The site's guide to the slavery texts, and the Reading the Law guide, go further.
passages.asks: The law said that a person who belongs to God cannot be owned by another. Ask whom you treat as though they existed for your use: at work, at home, among those who make what you buy. And ask where people are held or forced to work in your own country today, and what you could do about it.

passages.happening:
An Israelite may fall so low that he sells himself to a foreigner who has prospered in the land (verse 47). Even then, “he retains the right of redemption after he has sold himself. One of his brothers may redeem him” (verse 48). An uncle, a cousin or any close relative may do it, or he may redeem himself if he prospers (verse 49).

The price is worked out by the years left until the Jubilee (verses 50-52). His owner “must not rule over him harshly in your sight” (verse 53). “Even if he is not redeemed in any of these ways, he and his children shall be released in the Year of Jubilee” (verse 54).

“For the Israelites are My servants. They are My servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt. I am the LORD your God” (verse 55).
passages.hearers:
This is the last step down, and the law still follows the man with a way back.

His family is to come for him. The duty falls on the nearest relative who is able: a brother, an uncle, a cousin. This is the go'el again, the relative who redeems, now buying back a person. Family, in this chapter, is the first line of rescue.

The community is to watch. The owner must not treat him harshly ‘in your sight’. Israel is not to look away from what is done to one of its own.

And if no one comes, the Jubilee does. No Israelite's bondage could be handed on for ever.

The chapter ends where its argument has been heading. Twice in one verse God says, ‘They are My servants’. The Hebrew word, eved, is used for a slave, for a king's official and for a worshiper of God. Israel had been Pharaoh's slaves. It is now God's servants. That is the deepest reason it cannot be anyone else's.
passages.later:
The New Testament uses the language of redemption for what Christ has done. Peter writes that believers were redeemed, “not with perishable things such as silver or gold”, but with the blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18-19).

Paul draws the same conclusion this chapter draws: “You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of men” (1 Corinthians 7:23).
passages.asks: The law looked first to the family to buy a lost member back, and told the community not to look away. Ask who in your own family has drifted or fallen, and whether anyone has gone after them. And ask what it means to you that you belong to God, and so are not finally owned by anything else.
